Pastoral Theology
PAS-tuh-ruhl thee-OL-uh-jee
noun
From pastoral (of a shepherd) + theology; the discipline of the care and oversight of souls by the minister of Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

Pastoral theology is the discipline that treats the care and oversight of souls by the minister of Christ—the application of the whole counsel of God to the feeding, leading, guarding, and healing of the flock. Its model is the Good Shepherd, who gives His life for the sheep, knows them by name, seeks the lost, binds up the broken, and feeds them in green pastures; and its undershepherds, the elders, are charged to feed the flock of God which is among them, taking the oversight thereof not by constraint but willingly, not for filthy lucre but of a ready mind, neither as lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. The pastor’s chief work is the ministry of the Word—preaching, teaching, warning, comforting—joined to prayer, the administration of the ordinances, the visiting of the sick and the sorrowful, the admonition of the wayward, the comforting of the afflicted, and the watching for souls as one that must give account. The Reformed and Puritan tradition produced a rich literature of pastoral theology, of which Baxter’s Reformed Pastor is the great monument, pressing the minister to know and watch over every soul in his charge. The dictionary honors pastoral theology as the shepherd-care of souls after the pattern of the Chief Shepherd—the feeding, leading, guarding, and healing of the flock by the faithful minister of the Word—and presses both the high calling and the solemn account of those who watch for souls.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The discipline of the care and oversight of souls by the minister; the shepherd-care of the flock—feeding, leading, guarding, healing—after the Chief Shepherd’s pattern.

PASTORAL THEOLOGY, the care and oversight of souls by the minister.

Modeled on the Good Shepherd, who gives His life for the sheep.

Elders feed the flock, not as lords but as ensamples (1Pe 5:2-3).

📖 Key Scripture

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Heb 13:17 — "Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you."

Joh 21:16 — "He saith to him again the second time, Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me? He saith unto him, Yea, Lord; thou knowest that I love thee. He saith unto him, Feed my sheep."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Ministry is recast as professional management or therapeutic counsel; Scripture makes it the shepherd-care of souls by the Word, after the Chief Shepherd’s pattern.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond two drifts. The first recasts the ministry as professional management—the pastor as executive, the church as enterprise, success measured by numbers and programs. The second reduces pastoral care to therapeutic counsel, the minister a religious therapist tending felt needs with the wisdom of the age rather than the Word of God. Both displace the shepherd-care of souls by the truth, which is the heart of the office.

The principle to recover is the shepherd-care of souls after the pattern of the Chief Shepherd. The elders are charged to feed the flock of God, taking the oversight, not as lords but as ensamples (1 Pet 5:2-3), and to take heed to all the flock over which the Holy Ghost has made them overseers, to feed the church of God which He purchased with His own blood (Acts 20:28). The risen Lord’s thrice-repeated charge to Peter was, Feed my sheep (John 21:16). The pastor’s chief work is the ministry of the Word—preaching, warning, comforting—joined to prayer, the ordinances, and the watching over each soul. And the office carries a solemn account, for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account (Heb 13:17). Pastoral theology calls the minister back from the manager’s desk and the therapist’s couch to the shepherd’s staff and the Word of God.
